strengths: Novel framing of self-contradiction in MLLMs and the insight that capability asymmetry between generation and understanding can be leveraged for self-improvement
Comprehensive multi-perspective analysis combining empirical characterization, theoretical framework (Proposition 1 on aligned learning dynamics), and practical methods
Important discovery that internal metrics (Nonunified score) cannot distinguish co-degradation from co-improvement, with practical implications for safe self-improvement
Extensive empirical validation that results align with theoretical predictions (Figures 4, 8; Tables 1-2)
Clear motivation with compelling examples of self-contradiction in real MLLMs (Figure 1)
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only Janus-Pro models on T2I-CompBench with focus on 3D Spatial subtask; no evaluation on other unified architectures (Show-O, Chameleon, Emu3) or diverse benchmarks despite their relevance

Contradictory framing: method is presented as 'self-improvement without external supervision' but fundamentally depends on external oracle (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) for ground truth labels, validation, and avoiding co-degradation—no robustness analysis for oracle choice

Theoretical analysis significantly limited: single-token assumption (L=1), linear approximation case study, loose connection to transformer dynamics, and one-step analysis that doesn't explain multi-step training
Modest empirical improvements (5-10% gains in Table 3) reported without statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or ablation studies on curriculum components

WinRate metric measures agreement with external oracle rather than absolute understanding quality, and only ~60% of generation-improved samples follow predicted theoretical dynamics (Table 2), with inadequate explanation of discrepancies
Incomplete analysis of co-degradation: only observed in small Janus-1B model with severely corrupted data; practical prevalence unclear and solution requires external oracle anyway
Limited comparison with related work: T2I-R1 and concurrent methods (UniRL, HermesFlow) minimally discussed; position relative to other self-improvement approaches unclear
Missing key ablations: sensitivity to oracle choice, curriculum component contribution, scaling with dataset size, and failure case analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Self-contradiction in MLLMs is a clear and compelling observation with good intuitive examples. Insightful identification that unified models aren't truly unified.

Systematic analysis with principled methodology: Clear quantification via Nonunified score, careful decomposition of causes (85% weak generation vs. 15% weak understanding), and validation using external model (Qwen) for ground truth.

Novel theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 extends learning dynamics framework to multimodal setting in a non-trivial way, explaining aligned learning trajectories between generation and understanding branches. Case study provides good intuition.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Multiple post-training strategies tested (SFT, DPO, curriculum variants), co-improvement demonstrated across settings, learning dynamics predictions validated empirically, both in-distribution and OOD evaluation.

Honest discussion of limitations: Acknowledges and demonstrates co-degradation risk with poor data quality, shows intrinsic metrics cannot distinguish co-improvement from co-degradation, discusses model-size dependent phenomena, and identifies generalization as future work.

Technical soundness and rigor: Experimental design is solid with proper controls, detailed hyperparameters provided, external validation methodology is appropriate, ablations and sensitivity analyses included.

Practical relevance: Addresses real problem in unified MLLM design; findings would be valuable for practitioners; self-improvement without external supervision is appealing (though qualified by need for data validation).
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: Primarily focuses on Janus-Pro models with only brief comparison to T2I-R1. No evaluation on other unified architectures (Show-O, Chameleon, etc.) despite claiming insights about unified MLLMs generally. Limits confidence in generalizability of findings.

Metric design concerns: Nonunified score relies on potentially imperfect understanding branch as ground truth. Validation requires external Qwen-72B model, reducing practical appeal of 'self-improvement without external signals.' UniDet and WinRate are non-standard metrics with unclear correlation to human judgment or standard community benchmarks.

Theoretical limitations: Learning dynamics analysis restricted to single-token case (L=1) with extension to multi-token unaddressed. Connection between one-step dynamics and actual multi-epoch training behavior could be more rigorous. Some empirical validations are loose (~60% alignment threshold).

Straightforward methodology: Using understanding branch as DPO/SFT reward model is natural but not technically novel. Curriculum learning strategy applies standard easy-to-hard progression without novel insights. Main contributions are in analysis/discovery rather than new methods.

Co-degradation analysis limitations: Only demonstrated on weak 1B model with extreme corruption (fixed token). Unclear how critical for realistic scenarios. Proposed solution (external validation) undermines 'self-improvement' narrative. More realistic corruption patterns needed.

Modest empirical improvements: Improvements are typically 5-10%, which while consistent, are not dramatic. Performance gains may not justify additional computational cost of running understanding branch repeatedly.

Generalization and reproducibility gaps: All strong positive results on Janus-Pro; generalizability to other architectures unverified. Applicability to non-image modalities unclear. No mention of code release. Dependency on external models reduces reproducibility without additional resources.

Dense presentation in places: Learning dynamics section (3.2.1) is technically heavy with complex notation. Some key results (Figures 8-9) relegated to appendix. Figure 4 visualization could be clearer. Paper covers substantial ground but some sections feel rushed.

strengths: Identifies an important practical problem: non-unification in MLLMs with comprehensive empirical validation across 6 diverse architectures and multiple benchmarks, controlled for task difficulty confounders

Proposes a simple yet effective self-improvement framework without external signals that achieves up to 20% generation and 16% unification improvements, surpassing external-reward baselines (T2I-R1, HermesFlow)
Novel non-unification metric that measures internal consistency rather than relying on external evaluators, avoiding external bias

Sophisticated theoretical contribution: extends learning dynamics theory to multimodal setting with formal analysis (Propositions 1-2) explaining co-improvement via shared eNTK, supported by comprehensive empirical evidence (Figures 7, 13-16)
Empirically discovers and documents co-improvement effect in post-training (80% from false positive correction), an underexplored phenomenon
Rigorous empirical methodology with human evaluation validation, careful stratification by difficulty, and clear attribution to weak generation vs. misunderstanding
Excellent reproducibility: detailed algorithms, hyperparameter tables, complete results across benchmarks, and clear implementation details
weaknesses: Severely limited model coverage for self-improvement: only 2 models tested (Janus-Pro-7B and Show-o, both relatively small), with generalization to other architectures and larger models unverified; acknowledged but critical limitation

Theoretical analysis relies on questionable assumptions: uniform prompt prior (Eq. 7) is unrealistic, shared-tokenizer assumption doesn't match all architectures, first-order Taylor approximations may be loose, and eNTK sharing claims lack rigorous proof

Metric reliability concerns: Qwen-based evaluation shows 19.67% discrepancy on hard tasks undermining confidence in 'Weak Generation' classification for complex reasoning; non-unification score circularly depends on understanding quality
Conceptual novelty of method is limited: self-improvement reduces to using internal understanding as reward signal—not fundamentally different from external reward models except for the signal source
Circular reasoning in validation: improvements correlate with internal gap (ρ=0.53, Figure 4), meaning method works better where problem is worse, somewhat tautological
Small post-training datasets limit scalability: Janus-Pro 1,326 samples, Show-o 226; even with curriculum learning ~1,091 additions—tiny compared to pre-training scales and many samples remain unused
Statistical rigor issues: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; single-run results without seeds; small sample sizes for some benchmarks (Science-T2I: 49 chemistry examples)
Incomplete baseline comparisons: T2I-R1 only on Janus-Pro, HermesFlow only on Show-o; head-to-head comparisons on same models with same data lacking
Curriculum learning component feels ancillary: modest gains in Table 1 (C-SFT vs SFT), epoch 10 choice appears empirically driven without principled justification (Section F.2)

Limited scope: text-to-image only, English prompts only, understanding evaluation limited to alignment scoring; generalization to other modalities/reasoning tasks unclear; computational costs underspecified

strengths: Well-motivated problem with comprehensive verification of non-unification across 6 MLLMs and multiple benchmarks
Novel self-consistency metric (non-unification score) avoiding external evaluator bias
Extensive empirical work with consistent improvements (20% generation, 16% unification gains) across benchmarks
Interesting learning dynamics analysis extending to multimodal settings and explaining co-improvement via eNTK
Thorough presentation with extensive ablations, appendices, and additional results
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Self-improvement experiments limited to only 2 of 6 evaluated models (Janus-Pro, Show-o), severely limiting generalizability claims
Limited methodological novelty: core approach is straightforward self-training with internal quality filtering, incremental over existing techniques
Theory-practice mismatch: theory assumes shared tokenizers but main experiments use decoupled architectures (Janus-Pro); extension to decoupled case not rigorously proven
Theory analyzes one-step updates but training involves 20-30 epochs; empirical evidence is correlational rather than causal
Marginal curriculum learning results: Table 1 shows minimal gains over baseline SFT/DPO, contradicting motivation from co-improvement

Experimental concerns: weak generation attribution relies on potentially biased Qwen oracle; understanding eval uses circular logic (win rate on pre-trained outputs); human eval shows 19.67% disagreement on hard tasks
Insufficient failure analysis: no breakdown of when method fails, which prompt/image types benefit, or why moderate correlation (ρ=0.53) exists between gap size and improvement
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned, high computational cost (10 images/prompt × 6000 prompts), non-standard DPO modification not justified
Paper attempts too much (metric + method + theory + curriculum) without sufficient depth in any single area; tries to cover 6 models for gap verification but only 2 for method evaluation

Interesting theoretical contribution extending learning dynamics to multimodal setting with shared eNTK explanation for co-improvement; well-supported by empirical evidence across multiple models
Simple yet effective self-improvement framework combining understanding scores with standard post-training; easy to implement and reproduce
Excellent presentation with clear writing, informative figures, and comprehensive appendix including full proofs and derivations
Multi-dimensional contributions addressing problem characterization, practical solution, theoretical understanding, and method enhancement (curriculum learning)

weaknesses: Core self-improvement method is relatively straightforward (score candidates with understanding, apply SFT/DPO), representing application of existing techniques rather than novel methodology
